title: Debate in Brainstorming
text:
A core rule of classic brainstorming is that no one may criticize an idea, because judgment is supposed to stifle creativity. Charlan Nemeth and her colleagues doubted this. Her research on dissent had suggested that disagreement can stimulate thinking.

With Bernard Personnaz, Marie Personnaz and Jack Goncalo, she ran a study in the United States and in France. Small groups were asked to come up with ideas for reducing traffic congestion in their area. Groups received one of three sets of instructions: no special rules, the traditional brainstorming rules including a ban on criticism, or instructions to brainstorm but also to debate and even criticize each other's ideas.

The groups told to debate produced more ideas than the other groups, in both countries.

The authors argued that criticism, when it is about ideas, can push people to think harder and look further, rather than shutting them down.
lesson: Do not ban criticism in idea sessions. Encourage people to challenge ideas freely, as long as they attack the idea and not the person.
people: Charlan Nemeth, Bernard Personnaz, Marie Personnaz, Jack Goncalo
source: Nemeth, C. J., Personnaz, B., Personnaz, M., and Goncalo, J. A. (2004). The liberating role of conflict in group creativity: A study in two countries. European Journal of Social Psychology, 34(4), 365-374.
